passage:
For many decades, biologists believed that animal vision relied entirely on a single light-sensitive protein called rhodopsin. This protein, found in the eyes of vertebrates and invertebrates alike, absorbs photons of light and initiates a chain of chemical reactions that ultimately generates an electrical signal sent to the brain. The discovery of this mechanism seemed to explain vision comprehensively.

However, beginning in the 1980s, researchers identified additional light-sensitive proteins in the eyes of various organisms. These newly discovered proteins, termed opsins, were found to absorb light at different wavelengths from rhodopsin. Some opsins respond primarily to blue light, while others are most sensitive to red or green wavelengths. The presence of multiple opsins in a single organism suggested that animals could discriminate among colors by comparing signals from cells containing different opsins.

A striking example emerged from studies of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. Researchers discovered that fruit flies possess three types of opsins in their compound eyes, each tuned to detect different parts of the visible spectrum. By comparing the strength of signals from these three opsin types, the fruit fly's nervous system can construct a sophisticated color perception. This capability allows the fly to identify ripe fruit and locate potential mates on the basis of coloration, behaviors essential to its survival.

The finding that multiple opsins enable color vision has broad implications. It suggests that color perception evolved not as a single innovation but as a gradual accumulation of different light-sensing proteins. Furthermore, understanding these proteins has practical applications: researchers are now developing optogenetic tools that use engineered opsins to control neural activity in living organisms. These tools have become invaluable for studying how the brain processes sensory information.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rhodopsin is the most important light-sensitive protein in animal eyes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The discovery of multiple opsins revealed a more complex basis for animal color vision than previously understood.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fruit flies have better color vision than most other animals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Light-sensitive proteins have no application outside of basic vision research.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rhodopsin and opsins function in identical ways in all animal species.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the arc from the single-protein (rhodopsin) explanation to the discovery of multiple opsins that enable color discrimination. This is the central thesis.
explanations.A: The passage does not argue that rhodopsin is most important; rather, it highlights the role of additional opsins.
explanations.C: Fruit flies are an example, not the main point of the passage.
explanations.D: The passage mentions optogenetic applications, so this is directly contradicted.
explanations.E: The passage shows that different opsins respond to different wavelengths, so they do not function identically.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, what is the primary function of rhodopsin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To absorb photons of light and initiate a chain of chemical reactions that generates an electrical signal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To compare signals from cells containing different wavelength-sensitive proteins.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To allow animals to distinguish between ripe and unripe fruit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To enable the construction of optogenetic tools for neural research.

choices.label: E
choices.text: To facilitate color discrimination in compound eyes.

explanations.correct: The passage explicitly states in paragraph 1 that rhodopsin 'absorbs photons of light and initiates a chain of chemical reactions that ultimately generates an electrical signal sent to the brain.'
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This is the function of comparing multiple opsins, not rhodopsin alone.
explanations.C: This is a behavioral application enabled by color vision, not rhodopsin's function.
explanations.D: This describes applications of engineered opsins, not rhodopsin's basic function.
explanations.E: Color discrimination is enabled by multiple opsins in comparison, not by rhodopsin alone.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that animals without multiple opsins would likely have difficulty

choices.label: A
choices.text: detecting light of any wavelength.

choices.label: B
choices.text: distinguishing between objects of different colors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: transmitting electrical signals to the brain.

choices.label: D
choices.text: absorbing photons in low-light conditions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: responding to light in the infrared spectrum.

explanations.correct: The passage explains that by comparing signals from multiple opsins tuned to different wavelengths, animals can discriminate colors. Without multiple opsins, this comparison would not be possible, making color discrimination difficult.
explanations.A: The passage suggests that even a single opsin can detect light; the issue is discrimination among colors.
explanations.C: Even a single opsin initiates electrical signals; multiple opsins are not necessary for this.
explanations.D: The passage does not address the relationship between the number of opsins and light sensitivity in low-light conditions.
explanations.E: The passage discusses the visible spectrum, not infrared.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of fruit flies in the third paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that compound eyes are superior to simple eyes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide a concrete example of how multiple opsins enable color vision in a specific organism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: explain why fruit flies are more commonly studied than other insects.

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that color vision is essential for finding food and reproduction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that fruit flies perceive colors more accurately than humans do.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 illustrates the general principle from paragraph 2—that multiple opsins enable color discrimination—by describing the specific case of the fruit fly and its three opsins.
explanations.A: The passage does not argue that one eye type is superior.
explanations.C: The passage does not address the reasons for study frequency.
explanations.D: While the passage mentions these behaviors, the primary function here is to illustrate the mechanism of color vision in a specific organism.
explanations.E: The passage does not compare the accuracy of color perception across species.

explanations.C: The passage emphasizes the importance of the findings.
explanations.D: The passage describes optogenetic tools as 'invaluable.'

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following scenarios best illustrates the principle of color vision described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An organism possesses a single opsin that detects all wavelengths of visible light equally well.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: An organism uses its brain to interpret signals from opsins regardless of their light sensitivity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An organism relies on rhodopsin alone to identify the colors of potential food sources.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An organism's opsins absorb photons but fail to generate electrical signals.

explanations.correct: The passage explains that color vision arises from comparing signals from multiple opsins tuned to different wavelengths. Choice B directly instantiates this principle.
explanations.A: A single opsin detecting all wavelengths equally does not enable color discrimination through comparison.
explanations.C: While the brain does interpret signals, this choice ignores the key mechanism of comparing different opsins.
explanations.D: The passage shows that multiple opsins, not rhodopsin alone, enable color discrimination.
explanations.E: Non-functional opsins cannot enable color vision.

passage:
Coral reefs are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth, supporting an extraordinary diversity of marine life in tropical and subtropical waters. This productivity is surprising given that coral reefs thrive in waters that are often nutrient-poor. The key to this apparent paradox lies in the intimate relationship between corals and their symbiotic partners, photosynthetic algae called zooxanthellae.

Corals are animals that obtain energy primarily through a symbiotic relationship with zooxanthellae, which live within the coral's tissues. The algae use sunlight to produce sugars through photosynthesis, and these sugars sustain both the algae and their coral hosts. In return, the coral provides the zooxanthellae with a protected environment and access to nutrients extracted from the surrounding water. This exchange of resources is mutually beneficial: the algae receive shelter and a steady supply of inorganic nutrients, while the coral receives energy-rich sugars necessary for growth and reproduction.

The efficiency of this symbiosis allows corals to build massive reef structures despite the nutrient scarcity of their surroundings. Zooxanthellae are remarkably efficient at capturing solar energy and converting it to chemical energy in the form of sugars. Additionally, the algae's presence within the coral's tissues means that nutrients from fish waste and other organic matter are recycled internally rather than lost to the water column. This internal recycling system is crucial to the reef ecosystem's ability to sustain high levels of biodiversity.

Understanding the coral-zooxanthellae symbiosis has important implications for reef conservation. When water temperatures rise beyond the tolerance range of zooxanthellae, the algae are expelled from coral tissue in a process called coral bleaching. Without zooxanthellae, corals lose their primary energy source and eventually die. Recent studies have shown that protecting reef ecosystems requires addressing the environmental stressors that threaten this essential symbiotic relationship.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coral reefs are the most productive ecosystems in the world.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The symbiotic relationship between corals and zooxanthellae enables reef productivity and must be protected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zooxanthellae are photosynthetic organisms that live in tropical and subtropical waters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coral bleaching occurs when water temperatures become too warm for corals to survive.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nutrient recycling is the only factor that sustains coral reef ecosystems.

explanations.correct: The passage establishes the symbiosis as the foundation of reef productivity (paragraphs 1-3) and concludes by noting its importance for conservation (paragraph 4). This is the central thesis.
explanations.A: While the passage notes high productivity, it does not claim reefs are the most productive ecosystems overall.
explanations.C: This is a supporting detail, not the main point.
explanations.D: Coral bleaching is mentioned as an example of the symbiosis under threat, not the main point.
explanations.E: Nutrient recycling is one factor among several; the passage does not isolate it as the only sustaining factor.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, what does the coral provide to zooxanthellae?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Access to photosynthetic pathways and chemical energy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Protection and access to nutrients

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sugars and oxygen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sunlight and inorganic salts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Refuge from tropical water currents

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states explicitly: 'the coral provides the zooxanthellae with a protected environment and access to nutrients extracted from the surrounding water.'
explanations.A: The algae already have photosynthetic pathways; the coral does not provide these.
explanations.C: The algae produce sugars; the coral does not provide them. Oxygen is not mentioned.
explanations.D: Sunlight comes from the environment, not the coral; the coral does provide nutrient access but not inorganic salts directly.
explanations.E: The passage does not mention water currents.

questions.questionStem: Based on the passage, it can be inferred that a coral reef in a nutrient-rich environment would likely

choices.label: A
choices.text: have less need for the coral-zooxanthellae symbiosis than reefs in nutrient-poor waters.

choices.label: B
choices.text: produce larger zooxanthellae than reefs in nutrient-poor waters.

choices.label: C
choices.text: experience more frequent coral bleaching events.

choices.label: D
choices.text: require more extensive internal nutrient recycling.

choices.label: E
choices.text: support fewer species of algae than nutrient-poor reefs.

explanations.correct: The passage explains that the symbiosis is essential because reefs exist in nutrient-poor waters. By contrast, a nutrient-rich environment could provide energy and nutrients through other means, reducing the dependence on symbiosis.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage does not discuss zooxanthellae size.
explanations.C: Bleaching is related to temperature stress, not nutrient availability.
explanations.D: In a nutrient-rich environment, internal recycling would be less critical because external nutrients are available.
explanations.E: The passage does not address the number of algae species.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of coral bleaching in the final paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: explain the biochemical mechanism by which temperature affects zooxanthellae.

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate why understanding the symbiosis is important for protecting reefs from environmental threats.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that zooxanthellae are sensitive to all environmental changes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: prove that global warming is the greatest threat to coral reefs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that coral bleaching can be reversed if temperatures are lowered quickly.

explanations.correct: The final paragraph uses coral bleaching as an example of how environmental stress threatens the symbiosis, supporting the argument that reef conservation depends on protecting this relationship.
explanations.A: The passage describes what happens during bleaching, not the biochemical mechanism.
explanations.C: The passage mentions temperature sensitivity, not all environmental changes.
explanations.D: The passage does not claim global warming is the greatest threat overall.
explanations.E: The passage does not discuss reversibility.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, what is coral bleaching?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A process by which corals lose their color when zooxanthellae are expelled from coral tissue due to high water temperatures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A chemical reaction that occurs when water becomes too nutrient-rich.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The natural shedding of old zooxanthellae during the coral's growth cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An adaptation that allows corals to survive in cold water environments.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A disease that spreads rapidly through overcrowded reef ecosystems.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 4 defines coral bleaching: 'When water temperatures rise beyond the tolerance range of zooxanthellae, the algae are expelled from coral tissue in a process called coral bleaching.'
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage relates bleaching to temperature, not nutrient richness.
explanations.C: Bleaching is triggered by temperature stress, not a natural growth cycle.
explanations.D: The passage presents bleaching as harmful, not adaptive.
explanations.E: The passage does not characterize bleaching as a disease.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the importance of the coral-zooxanthellae relationship can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismissive of its role in reef productivity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: uncertain about whether it truly benefits both organisms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: convinced of its fundamental importance to reef ecosystems and their survival.

choices.label: D
choices.text: skeptical that environmental stressors can disrupt the relationship.

choices.label: E
choices.text: indifferent to the implications for reef conservation.

explanations.correct: The passage presents the symbiosis as the foundation of reef productivity and emphasizes that protecting it is essential for reef conservation. The author treats it as fundamental and vital.
explanations.A: The passage emphasizes the relationship's central importance to reef productivity.
explanations.B: The passage clearly establishes that the relationship is mutually beneficial.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage describes coral bleaching as a real threat to the relationship.
explanations.E: The passage concludes with explicit conservation implications.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A paradox is introduced, the symbiotic mechanism that resolves it is explained, and the implications for conservation are noted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A scientific hypothesis is presented, tested, and then rejected in favor of an alternative explanation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Multiple examples of coral reef ecosystems are described and compared across geographic regions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A historical overview of coral reef research is provided, followed by a discussion of current findings.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The evolution of zooxanthellae is traced from simple to complex forms across geological time.

explanations.correct: The passage opens by posing a paradox (productivity in nutrient-poor waters), explains the mechanism (symbiosis) in paragraphs 2-3, and concludes with conservation implications in paragraph 4.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No hypothesis is tested or rejected; the explanation is straightforward.
explanations.C: The passage does not compare different reef regions.
explanations.D: No historical overview is provided.
explanations.E: The passage does not address evolutionary history.

passage:
The discovery of gravitational waves in 2015 represents a landmark achievement in physics, confirming a prediction made by Albert Einstein a century earlier. Gravitational waves are ripples in space-time itself, propagating at the speed of light. They are produced by the acceleration of massive objects, such as colliding black holes or merging neutron stars. Before 2015, gravitational waves remained theoretical; physicists had never directly detected them.

The challenge of detecting gravitational waves stems from their extreme weakness. When gravitational waves pass through Earth, they cause minuscule distortions in space-time—changes so small that a detector would need to measure distances to a precision of one part in ten quintillion (10,000,000,000,000,000). To achieve this sensitivity, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) employs an ingenious design: two perpendicular tunnels, each several kilometers long, with mirrors at each end. A laser beam is split and sent down both tunnels simultaneously. When no gravitational waves are present, the laser beams travel equal distances and recombine in phase, canceling each other out.

However, when a gravitational wave passes through the detector, it stretches space along one tunnel and compresses it along the other. This differential distortion causes the laser beams to travel slightly different distances and therefore to recombine out of phase. The resulting interference pattern—a subtle shift in the light signal—reveals the passage of a gravitational wave. Sophisticated statistical analysis is then applied to confirm that the detected signal is genuine rather than instrumental noise.

The 2015 detection came from the collision of two black holes approximately 1.3 billion light-years away. The event itself lasted only a fraction of a second, yet it generated gravitational waves detectable across the entire galaxy. This achievement opened a new window on the universe, enabling astronomers to observe phenomena that emit gravitational waves but little or no light. The success of LIGO has motivated international collaborations to build new detectors, expanding our ability to map the violent and exotic events occurring throughout the cosmos.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Albert Einstein predicted gravitational waves, but his theory remained unproven until the twenty-first century.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The detection of gravitational waves through LIGO technology has confirmed Einstein's prediction and opened new observational possibilities in astronomy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gravitational waves are caused exclusively by the collision of black holes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory is the only instrument capable of detecting space-time distortions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gravitational waves travel at the speed of light and can be measured with perfect accuracy.

explanations.correct: The passage traces the arc from Einstein's century-old prediction to the 2015 detection, explaining LIGO's method and the significance of the achievement for astronomy. This is the central thesis.
explanations.A: Einstein made the prediction, not left it unproven; the passage discusses the 2015 confirmation.
explanations.C: The passage mentions that gravitational waves can be produced by merging neutron stars and other accelerating massive objects, not just black holes.
explanations.D: The passage notes that LIGO's success motivated the building of new detectors, suggesting others exist.
explanations.E: While the passage states gravitational waves travel at light speed, it does not claim they can be measured with perfect accuracy; the precision is finite.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, what is the primary mechanism by which LIGO detects gravitational waves?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Measuring changes in the intensity of light emitted by distant black holes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Using perpendicular tunnels and mirrors to detect differential distortions in space-time through interference patterns in laser beams.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Analyzing electromagnetic radiation produced by colliding stars.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Directly measuring the speed at which gravitational waves travel through space.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Observing the light signals that accompany the merger of neutron stars.

explanations.correct: Paragraphs 2 and 3 explain that LIGO splits a laser beam, sends it down perpendicular tunnels, and detects interference patterns caused by differential distortions in space-time.
explanations.A: LIGO does not measure light from black holes; it detects space-time distortions.
explanations.C: LIGO detects space-time distortions, not electromagnetic radiation.
explanations.D: The passage states that gravitational waves travel at the speed of light but does not describe direct measurement of that speed as LIGO's mechanism.
explanations.E: LIGO detects gravitational waves, not the light signals that may accompany mergers.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that the reason gravitational waves were not detected before 2015 was that

choices.label: A
choices.text: physicists did not believe gravitational waves actually existed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the technology required to measure such small distortions in space-time did not exist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: there were no gravitational wave-producing events occurring in the universe before 2015.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Einstein's theory was later proven to be incorrect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gravitational waves travel too slowly to be observed by conventional instruments.

explanations.correct: The passage explains that gravitational waves are extremely weak and require extraordinary precision to detect. The description of LIGO's sophisticated technology implies that earlier instruments lacked the necessary sensitivity.
explanations.A: The passage states the waves remained 'theoretical,' suggesting belief in them, not disbelief.
explanations.C: Black hole collisions and neutron star mergers have always occurred; the issue was detection, not occurrence.
explanations.D: The passage confirms Einstein's prediction; his theory was not proven incorrect.
explanations.E: The passage states gravitational waves travel at the speed of light, not slowly.

questions.questionStem: The author's description of the 2015 gravitational wave detection event in the fourth paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide a historical chronology of all gravitational wave detections to date.

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate the practical application of LIGO technology and illustrate its significance for observational astronomy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: explain why black holes emit more gravitational waves than other cosmic objects.

choices.label: D
choices.text: show that the collision of black holes is the only source of detectable gravitational waves.

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that further detections are unnecessary because the theory has been confirmed.

explanations.correct: The final paragraph describes the 2015 detection as a concrete example of LIGO's capability and emphasizes how it opened new observational possibilities, illustrating the achievement's significance.
explanations.A: The passage mentions only the 2015 detection, not a chronology of all detections.
explanations.C: The passage does not compare the emission rates of gravitational waves from different objects.
explanations.D: The passage mentions that gravitational waves are produced by merging neutron stars as well.
explanations.E: The passage states that LIGO's success motivated further detector construction, not that further detections are unnecessary.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, what happens to laser beams inside LIGO when a gravitational wave passes through the detector?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both beams are absorbed by the mirrors at the end of the tunnels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They travel equal distances and cancel each other out completely.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They travel different distances due to differential distortion and recombine out of phase, creating an interference pattern.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are deflected away from their tunnels by the gravitational wave.

choices.label: E
choices.text: They increase in speed as they travel down the lengthened tunnel.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 explains that when a gravitational wave passes through, it stretches space along one tunnel and compresses it along the other, causing the beams to travel different distances and recombine out of phase.
explanations.A: The beams are reflected by mirrors, not absorbed.
explanations.B: This describes what happens when no gravitational wave is present.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The beams remain in their tunnels; the gravitational wave distorts space rather than deflecting the beams.
explanations.E: The passage does not indicate that beam speed changes.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the 2015 gravitational wave detection can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: skeptical of the reliability of the LIGO results.

choices.label: B
choices.text: viewing it as a significant scientific achievement with important implications.

choices.label: C
choices.text: doubtful that further gravitational wave detections will be possible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: concerned that the detection may have been caused by instrumental error.

choices.label: E
choices.text: indifferent to the discovery's relevance for astronomy.

explanations.correct: The passage describes the detection as a 'landmark achievement' and emphasizes it 'opened a new window on the universe,' indicating the author views it as significant and consequential.
explanations.A: The passage does not express skepticism; it treats the detection as confirmed.
explanations.C: The passage mentions building new detectors, suggesting further detections are expected.
explanations.D: The passage mentions statistical analysis to confirm the signal is genuine, not expressing residual concern.
explanations.E: The passage explicitly discusses implications for observational astronomy.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following scenarios would most likely produce a detectable gravitational wave according to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A slowly rotating neutron star in stable orbit around a companion star.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two neutron stars spiraling toward each other and eventually merging.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A black hole moving at constant velocity through empty space.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A planet orbiting a star in a circular, unchanging path.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A stationary black hole at the center of a galaxy.

explanations.correct: The passage states that gravitational waves are produced by 'the acceleration of massive objects, such as colliding black holes or merging neutron stars.' Two merging neutron stars represent accelerating massive objects.
explanations.A: Slow rotation and stable orbit involve minimal acceleration.
explanations.C: Constant velocity involves no acceleration; gravitational waves require acceleration.
explanations.D: Circular, unchanging orbits involve no acceleration of the individual bodies.
explanations.E: A stationary black hole is not accelerating.
